messages.content: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository in Spring?

All three are stereotype annotations that register a class as a Spring bean via component scanning. @Component is the generic one. @Service marks the business-logic layer and adds no behavior, only intent. @Repository marks the persistence layer and additionally enables exception translation, converting vendor-specific persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy.
Explain the difference between Propagation.REQUIRED and Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW in @Transactional.

REQUIRED (the default) joins the existing transaction if there is one, otherwise it starts a new one. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a fresh, independent one. If the inner transaction commits and the outer one later rolls back, the inner work stays committed. Use REQUIRES_NEW for things like audit logging that must persist even when the caller fails.
What is the N+1 problem in JPA and how do you fix it?

The N+1 problem happens when you load N parent entities with one query and then lazily access a relation on each, triggering N additional queries. Fixes: use JOIN FETCH in JPQL, use @EntityGraph on the repository method, or set a batch size (hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) so lazy loads are grouped into IN queries. Enable SQL logging to detect it early.
What bean scopes does Spring support and which is the default?

The default scope is singleton: one shared instance per application context. Other scopes are prototype (a new instance every time the bean is requested) and, in web applications, request, session, application and websocket. Note that injecting a prototype bean into a singleton only creates it once, so use ObjectProvider or a scoped proxy if you need a fresh instance each time.
Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?

Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and lets you declare them final, so the object is immutable and always fully initialized. It is easy to unit test because you can pass mocks without a Spring container or reflection. It also exposes design problems: a constructor with too many parameters signals a class doing too much. Circular dependencies fail fast at startup instead of hiding. Since Spring 4.3, a single constructor needs no @Autowired.
How do you handle exceptions globally in a Spring Boot REST API?

Create a class annotated with @RestControllerAdvice and add methods annotated with @ExceptionHandler for each exception type. Each method returns a ResponseEntity with an appropriate HTTP status and a consistent error body, for example a timestamp, message and path. Spring 6 and Boot 3 also support ProblemDetail (RFC 7807) for standardized error responses. This keeps controllers free of try/catch blocks.
How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?

@SpringBootApplication includes @EnableAutoConfiguration, which loads the auto-configuration classes listed in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (older versions used spring.factories). Each class is guarded by @Conditional annotations such as @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean and @ConditionalOnProperty, so it only applies when the relevant library is on the classpath and you have not defined your own bean. Run with --debug to see the conditions report.
What is the default fetch type for JPA relationships?

For to-one relationships (@ManyToOne and @OneToOne) the default is EAGER. For to-many relationships (@OneToMany and @ManyToMany) the default is LAZY. Eager loading on to-one associations often causes unnecessary joins or extra queries, so a common practice is to set fetch = FetchType.LAZY explicitly and load related data only when needed, using JOIN FETCH or entity graphs.
Why does calling a @Transactional method from another method in the same class not start a transaction?

Spring implements @Transactional with AOP proxies. A call from outside goes through the proxy, which starts the transaction. A self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy, so the annotation is ignored. Fixes: move the method to another bean, inject the bean into itself or use AopContext.currentProxy(), or use TransactionTemplate for programmatic control. Also note the method must be public for proxy-based transactions to apply.
Does @Transactional roll back on checked exceptions?

No. By default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and its subclasses) and Errors. A checked exception such as IOException lets the transaction commit. To roll back on checked exceptions, specify @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class), or rollbackFor with the specific type.
